By varying the structural parameters of the photonic crystal slabs, multiple chiral EPs are identified near the Γ point, with their evolution and annihilation processes systematically analyzed. Furthermore, the pronounced transmission asymmetry observed near the EP enables polarization conversion from linear to circular, functioning as a quarter-wave plate. This approach provides a straightforward method for realizing and controlling chiral EPs in momentum space, thereby expanding the potential for practical applications in optical metadevices.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a method to create multiple chiral exceptional points near the Γ point in photonic crystal slabs, enabling polarization conversion.
motivation: Exceptional points in optical systems have unique topological properties; the goal is to achieve and control chiral scattering EPs in momentum space for practical applications.
method: The authors vary structural parameters of photonic crystal slabs and analyze topological evolution in momentum space to identify chiral EPs near the Γ point.
result: Multiple chiral EPs are identified, their evolution and annihilation are analyzed, and transmission asymmetry near the EP enables linear-to-circular polarization conversion.
conclusion: This approach provides a straightforward method for realizing and controlling chiral EPs, expanding potential for optical metadevices.

title: Integrated Error-suppressed Pipeline For Quantum Optimization Of Nontrivial Binary Combinatorial Optimization Problems On Gate-model Hardware At The 156-qubit Scale
authors: Natasha Sachdeva, Gavin S Hartnett, Smarak Maity, Samuel Marsh, Yulun Wang, Adam Winick, Ryan Dougherty, Daniel Canuto, You Quan Chong, G Adam Cox, Michael Hush, Pranav S Mundada, Christopher D B Bentley, Michael J Biercuk And Yuval Baum
abstract: We introduce a novel hybrid quantum–classical variational optimization method for unconstrained binary combinatorial optimization problems on gate-model quantum computers, integrating a custom variational ansatz, staged feedback-based dual variational parameter update strategies, efficient parametric compilation, automated error suppression during hardware execution, and scalable O( ) classical post-processing to correct for bitflip errors. Without this integrated approach, we show that standard circuit execution at scale produces output indistinguishable from random sampling, establishing the necessity of each pipeline component. We benchmark the method on IBM superconducting quantum computers for several optimization problems drawn from NP-hard problem classes, where the optimization is conducted on hardware with no use of classical simulation or prior knowledge of the solution. For Max-Cut on random regular graphs with topologies not matched to device connectivity, the method achieves approximation ratios (AR) of 100% for unweighted 3-regular graphs up to 156 nodes, weighted regular graphs up to 80 nodes, and weighted 7-regular graphs up 50 nodes. Applied to higher-order binary optimization, the method finds the ground state energy of 127- and 156-qubit spin-glass models matched to device topology with linear, quadratic, and cubic interaction terms, achieving ARs of at least 99.5% across all instances tested. The method consistently outperforms a classical local solver across all problems. Where published results on identical problem instances are available, our method demonstrates competitive or superior performance. These results demonstrate that an appropriately engineered variational approach enables gate-model quantum computers to produce high-quality solutions for binary optimization problems drawn from NP-hard problem classes at the 156-qubit scale, where naïve implementations are insufficient for good performance.
tldr: This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical variational optimization pipeline for binary combinatorial problems on gate-model quantum computers, achieving high approximation ratios on up to 156 qubits.
motivation: To demonstrate that gate-model quantum computers can solve NP-hard binary optimization problems at scale with an integrated error-suppressed pipeline, overcoming the limitations of naive implementations.
method: The method combines a custom variational ansatz, staged feedback-based dual variational parameter updates, efficient parametric compilation, automated error suppression, and scalable classical post-processing for bitflip error correction.
result: The pipeline achieves 100% approximation ratios for Max-Cut on unweighted 3-regular graphs up to 156 nodes and at least 99.5% for spin-glass models up to 156 qubits, outperforming classical local solvers.
conclusion: An appropriately engineered variational approach enables gate-model quantum computers to produce high-quality solutions for binary optimization problems at the 156-qubit scale, but the paper does not directly address the user's specific research interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, quantum communication, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Geometry-resolved Suppression Of Patch-potential Heating In Skeleton-electrode Ion Traps
authors: Chon-Teng Belmiro Chu, Hao-Chung Chen, Ting Hsu, Hsiang-Yu Lo, Ming-Shien Chang And Guin-Dar Lin
abstract: We present a quantitative, geometry-resolved framework to evaluate the effects of patch-potential noise in realistic three-dimensional Paul-trap structures. As a concrete application, we analyze a skeleton-electrode architecture and compare its performance against a conventional blade trap under identical ion-to-electrode distances and matched confinement parameters. The skeleton geometry achieves a suppression of motional heating exceeding 50%, with heating rate ratios of for the axial mode and for the radial mode. Patch-by-patch heating maps reveal that over 99% of the noise contribution originates from electrode surfaces within 500 m of the ion. We identify that axial heating follows a non-monotonic profile, with dominant ‘hotspots’ located at an intermediate distance of approximately 110 m. This behavior is driven by the vectorial directionality of the electric-field components, which provide the strongest axial coupling at these intermediate regions. Guided by these maps, we demonstrate a proof-of-principle electrode reconfiguration where segmented gaps are aligned with identified hotspots. This strategy successfully reduces axial heating even when the total electrode surface area increases, confirming that the spatial distribution of noise coupling—rather than total conductor area—is the primary driver of motional heating. These findings establish geometry-guided design as a practical route to suppress heating in trapped-ion platform, and the proposed skeleton architecture is compatible with advanced fabrication techniques, including metal additive manufacturing.
tldr: This paper presents a geometry-resolved framework to evaluate patch-potential heating in ion traps, demonstrating that skeleton-electrode designs can suppress motional heating by over 50% compared to conventional blade traps.
motivation: Motional heating from patch potentials is a major decoherence source in trapped-ion quantum computing. The authors aimed to understand the spatial origin of heating and design electrode geometries to mitigate it.
method: They developed a quantitative framework to compute patch-potential noise in realistic 3D Paul traps, applied it to a skeleton-electrode architecture and a conventional blade trap, and generated patch-by-patch heating maps to identify hotspots.
result: The skeleton geometry suppresses heating by >50% (axial mode 0.52, radial mode 0.48 relative to blade trap). Over 99% of noise comes from electrodes within 500 μm of the ion, and axial heating has a non-monotonic profile with hotspots at ~110 μm. Reconfiguring electrode gaps to align with hotspots reduces axial heating even with increased surface area.
conclusion: Geometry-guided design, specifically the skeleton architecture, is a practical route to suppress heating in ion traps, and the approach is compatible with advanced fabrication like metal additive manufacturing.

title: Probing A Theoretical Framework For A Photonic Extreme Learning Machine
authors: Vicente Rocha, Duarte Silva, Felipe C Moreira, Catarina S Monteiro, Tiago D Ferreira And Nuno A Silva
abstract: The development of computing paradigms alternative to von Neumann architectures has recently fueled significant progress in novel all-optical processing solutions. In this work, we investigate how the coherence properties can be exploited for computing by expanding information onto a higher-dimensional space in the photonic extreme learning machine framework. A theoretical framework is provided based on the transmission matrix formalism, mapping the input plane onto the output camera plane, resulting in the establishment of the connection with complex extreme learning machines and derivation of upper bounds for the hidden space dimensionality as well as the form of the activation functions. Experiments using free-space propagation through a diffusive medium, performed in low-dimensional input space regimes, validate the model and the proposed estimator for the dimensionality. Overall, the framework presented and the findings enclosed have the potential to foster further research in a multitude of directions, from the development of robust general-purpose all-optical hardware to a full-stack integration with optical sensing devices toward edge computing solutions.
tldr: This paper presents a theoretical framework for a photonic extreme learning machine using free-space propagation through a diffusive medium, focusing on coherence properties and dimensionality expansion.
motivation: To develop alternative computing paradigms beyond von Neumann architectures by exploiting optical coherence for all-optical processing.
method: The authors use a transmission matrix formalism to map input to output planes, derive upper bounds for hidden space dimensionality, and validate with experiments using free-space propagation through a diffusive medium.
result: The model connects to complex extreme learning machines and provides an estimator for dimensionality; experiments in low-dimensional input spaces validate the framework.
conclusion: The framework may foster development of all-optical hardware and edge computing solutions, but the paper is primarily about optical computing and not directly related to the user's research interests.

title: Emergent Hydrodynamics Of Chiral Active Fluids: Vortices, Bubbles And Odd Diffusion
authors: Umberto Marini Bettolo Marconi, Alessandro Petrini, Raphael Maire And Lorenzo Caprini
abstract: Starting from a microscopic multiparticle Langevin equation, we obtain a hydrodynamic description in terms of density and momentum fields for chiral active particles interacting via standard repulsive and nonlocal odd forces. These odd interactions are reciprocal but non-conservative: they are non-potential forces, as they act perpendicular to the vector joining any pair of particles. As a result, the torques that two particles exert on one another are non-reciprocal. The ensuing macroscopic continuum description consists of a continuity equation for the density and a generalized compressible Navier–Stokes equation for the fluid velocity. The latter includes a chirality-induced torque density term and an odd viscosity contribution. Our theory predicts the emergence of odd diffusivity, edge currents, and is consistent with an inhomogeneous phase—characterized by bubble-like structures—recently observed in simulations. Specifically, the theory exhibits a linear instability arising from the interplay between odd viscosity and torque density, and admits steady-state inhomogeneous solutions featuring bubbles and vortices, in qualitative agreement with numerical simulations. Our findings can be tested experimentally in systems of granular spinners or rotating microorganisms suspended in a fluid.
tldr: This paper derives a hydrodynamic theory for chiral active fluids with odd interactions, predicting odd diffusion, edge currents, and bubble-like structures.
motivation: To understand the collective behavior of chiral active particles (e.g., granular spinners, rotating microorganisms) and explain emergent patterns like vortices and bubbles observed in simulations.
method: Starting from a microscopic multiparticle Langevin equation with repulsive and odd forces, the authors derive macroscopic continuity and Navier–Stokes equations using standard coarse-graining techniques.
result: The theory reveals odd viscosity, odd diffusivity, and a linear instability leading to inhomogeneous steady states with bubbles and vortices, matching simulations.
conclusion: The findings provide a theoretical framework for chiral active fluids and can be tested experimentally, but the paper does not address quantum or information-theoretic aspects.

title: Probing Electron Correlations In Solids With Auger-photoelectron Coincidence Spectroscopy
authors: Roberto Gotter And Giovanni Stefani Robert A Bartynski
abstract: Auger photoelectron coincidence spectroscopy (APECS) has emerged as a powerful tool for probing electron–electron correlation in solids. When a photoexcited core hole decays via a core-valence-valence Auger transition, two valence holes are created in the final state. Consequently, the line shape of the Auger electron spectrum is influenced by both Coulomb and exchange interactions between the two holes. By simultaneously detecting the photoelectron and Auger electron emitted from a single photoionization event, APECS measurements place constraints on the two final state holes, enabling one to independently measure Coulomb and exchange correlation energies. This review highlights the key advantages of APECS over other electron spectroscopic techniques including separating overlapping spectral features, removing the background signal from inelastically scattered electrons, enhanced surface sensitivity and site specificity. It also cites examples of how these attributes can be used to investigate the properties of solids in an unprecedented manner. To aid in understanding APECS data and assist in experimental design, a phenomenological model for the probability of electron pair emission as a function of the photo- and Auger electron kinetic energies and emission angles is presented. The model is applied to a hypothetical solid, demonstrating how the contribution to APECS spectrum of final states with different spin configurations depends on these experimental parameters. A summary of results obtained by performing one-dimensional (as a function of Auger [EA] or photoelectron [EP] kinetic energy), two-dimensional (parallel detection of EAand EP) and angle-resolved (AR) (as a function of EA at specific photo- and Auger electron emission angles) APECS measurements is presented. In particular, measurements of ferromagnetic metals and antiferromagnetic transition metal oxides demonstrate how AR-APECS is a powerful tool for independently measuring Coulomb and exchange correlation energies. Finally, potential future applications of APECS and further developments of this experimental technique are discussed.
tldr: This paper reviews Auger-photoelectron coincidence spectroscopy (APECS) as a technique to probe electron correlations in solids, focusing on Coulomb and exchange interactions in valence holes.
motivation: To demonstrate the advantages of APECS over conventional electron spectroscopies for studying electron-electron correlations in solids, particularly for separating overlapping spectral features and enhancing surface sensitivity.
method: The paper presents a phenomenological model for the probability of electron pair emission as a function of kinetic energies and angles, and reviews experimental results from one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and angle-resolved APECS measurements.
result: APECS enables independent measurement of Coulomb and exchange correlation energies, as demonstrated in ferromagnetic metals and antiferromagnetic transition metal oxides.
conclusion: APECS is a powerful tool for probing electron correlations, with potential future applications in studying complex materials and further experimental developments.

title: Observation Of Custodial Chiral Symmetry In Memristive Topological Circuits
authors: Wenhao Li, Junyao Wu, Ning Han, Rui Zhao, Fujia Chen, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Zhen Gao, Ce Shang And Yihao Yang
abstract: The concept of custodial symmetry, a residual symmetry that protects physical observables from large quantum corrections, has been a cornerstone of high-energy physics. In classical engineered systems, however, experimental realization and observation of its classical analog have remained unexplored. Building on recent theoretical work (2022 Phys. Rev. Lett.128 097701), we report the first experimental observation of a classical analog of custodial chiral symmetry in a memristive Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) circuit. We provide direct experimental evidence for custodial symmetry by measuring the correction to the Lagrangian. This Lagrangian correction, which mimics a mass term in field theory, vanishes smoothly as the perturbation is reduced. We also demonstrate that topological edge states in the memristive SSH circuit remain localized at the boundary, consistent with custodial chiral symmetry. This work opens new avenues for emulating field-theoretic symmetries and nonlinear dynamics in memristive platforms.
tldr: This paper reports the first experimental observation of a classical analog of custodial chiral symmetry in a memristive Su–Schrieffer–Heeger circuit.
motivation: Custodial symmetry is a key concept in high-energy physics, but its classical analog had not been experimentally realized. The authors aimed to demonstrate this symmetry in a classical engineered system.
method: The authors built a memristive SSH circuit and measured the Lagrangian correction to observe the vanishing of the mass-like term as perturbation is reduced, and verified topological edge state localization.
result: They provided direct experimental evidence for custodial chiral symmetry by showing that the Lagrangian correction vanishes smoothly with perturbation, and that topological edge states remain localized.
conclusion: This work opens new avenues for emulating field-theoretic symmetries and nonlinear dynamics in memristive platforms, but is not directly related to the user's research interests.

title: 2d Excitonics With Atomically Thin Lateral Heterostructures
authors: S Shradha, R Rosati, H Lamsaadi, J Picker, I Paradisanos, Md T Hossain, L Krelle, L F Oswald, N Engel, D I Markina, K Watanabe, T Taniguchi, P K Sahoo, L Lombez, X Marie, P Renucci, V Paillard, J-M Poumirol, A Turchanin, E Malic And B Urbaszek
abstract: Semiconducting transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), such as MoSe2 and WSe2, exhibit unique optical and electronic properties. Vertical stacking of layers of one or more TMDs, to create heterostructures, has expanded the fields of moiré physics and twistronics. Bottom-up fabrication techniques, such as chemical vapor deposition, have advanced the creation of heterostructures beyond what was possible with mechanical exfoliation and stacking. These techniques now enable the fabrication of lateral heterostructures (LHs), where two or more monolayers are covalently bonded in the plane of their atoms. At their atomically sharp interfaces, lateral heterostructures exhibit additional phenomena, such as the formation of charge-transfer excitons, in which the electron and hole reside on opposite sides of the interface. Due to the energy landscape created by differences in the band structures of the constituent materials, unique effects such as unidirectional exciton transport and excitonic lensing can be observed in LHs. This review outlines recent progress in exciton dynamics and spectroscopy of TMD-based LHs and offers an outlook on future developments in excitonics in this promising system.
tldr: This review covers exciton dynamics and spectroscopy in atomically thin lateral heterostructures of transition metal dichalcogenides.
motivation: To summarize recent progress in 2D excitonics using lateral heterostructures, which offer unique exciton transport and lensing effects.
method: Review of experimental and theoretical studies on TMD-based lateral heterostructures, focusing on exciton dynamics and spectroscopy.
result: Lateral heterostructures exhibit charge-transfer excitons, unidirectional exciton transport, and excitonic lensing at atomically sharp interfaces.
conclusion: The field is promising for future excitonic devices, but the paper does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Fractionalized Fermi Liquids And The Cuprate Phase Diagram
authors: Pietro M Bonetti, Maine Christos, Alexander Nikolaenko, Aavishkar A Patel And Subir Sachdev
abstract: We review a theoretical framework for the cuprate superconductors, rooted in a fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL*) description of the intermediate-temperature pseudogap phase at low doping. The FL* theory predicted hole pockets each of fractional area at hole doping p, in contrast to the area in spin density wave theory. Magnetotransport measurements, including observation of the Yamaji angle, show clear evidence of hole pocket quasiparticles which can tunnel coherently between square lattice layers, and are consistent with the FL* description. The FL* phase of a single-band model is described using a layer construction with a pair of ancilla qubits on each site: the Ancilla layer model (ALM). Its mean field theory yields hole pockets of area , and matches the gapped photoemission spectrum in the anti-nodal region of the Brillouin zone. Fluctuations are described by the SU(2) gauge theory of a background spin liquid with critical Dirac spinons. A Monte Carlo study of the thermal SU(2) gauge theory transforms the hole pockets into Fermi arcs in photoemission. One route to confinement of FL* upon lowering temperature yields a d-wave superconductor via a Kosterlitz–Thouless transition of vortices, with nodal Bogoliubov quasiparticles featuring anisotropic velocities and vortices surrounded by charge order halos. An alternative route yields a charge-ordered metallic state that has quantum oscillations consistent with observations. These confinement transitions are driven by the condensation of a SU(2) fundamental Higgs field, which also provides a fractionalized description of intertwined orders. Increasing doping from the FL* phase in the ALM drives a transition to a conventional FL at large doping, passing through an intermediate strange metal regime. We formulate a theory of the FL*-FL metal-metal transition without a symmetry-breaking order parameter, using a critical quantum ‘charge’ liquid of mobile electrons in the presence of disorder, developed via an extension of the Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev model to two spatial dimensions. At low temperatures, and across optimal and over doping, we address the regimes of extended non-FL behavior by Griffiths effects near quantum phase transitions in disordered metals. Partly based on lectures by S S at Boulder School 2025, Dynamics of Strongly Correlated Electrons, 14–18 July. Lecture videos. Joint ICTP-WE Heraeus School and Workshop on Advances in Quantum Matter: Pushing the Boundaries, ICTP, Trieste, 4, 6 August 2025. Lecture videos. School on Quantum Dynamics of Matter, Light and Information, ICTP, Trieste, 18, 19 August 2025. Lecture videos. Croucher Advanced Study Institute for Fractional Chern Insulators, University of Hong Kong, 4, 5 September 2025. Lecture slides. Advanced School and Conference on Quantum Matter, ICTP Trieste, 1–12 December 2025. Lecture Notes. Lecture videos.
tldr: This paper reviews a theoretical framework for cuprate superconductors based on fractionalized Fermi liquids, focusing on the pseudogap phase and phase diagram.
motivation: To explain the anomalous properties of cuprate superconductors, particularly the pseudogap phase and the transition to strange metal behavior.
method: Theoretical review using the Ancilla layer model (ALM), SU(2) gauge theory, and extensions of the Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev model to two dimensions.
result: The FL* theory predicts hole pockets of fractional area, matches photoemission and magnetotransport data, and describes confinement transitions to d-wave superconductivity or charge order.
conclusion: The framework provides a unified description of the cuprate phase diagram, but the paper is a review and does not present new results.

tldr: This paper uses differential dynamic microscopy to detect Lévy flights in cells, a method for analyzing active particle motion.
motivation: Detecting Lévy flights in experiments is challenging due to the need for data across large spatiotemporal scales; the authors aim to demonstrate that differential dynamic microscopy can reliably extract power-law scaling.
method: Differential dynamic microscopy (DDM) is applied to analyze the motion of active Lévy particles, extracting the characteristic power-law exponent from the intermediate scattering function.
result: DDM successfully detects Lévy flight behavior and quantifies the power-law exponent, providing a robust experimental technique for studying such anomalous diffusion.
conclusion: The method offers a practical tool for studying Lévy flights in biological and soft matter systems, with potential applications in cell motility research.

tldr: This paper studies instability in queues where arrivals are governed by a search process with stochastic resetting, focusing on resource management in random environments.
motivation: To understand how stochastic resetting in search processes affects queue stability, relevant to natural and artificial resource management systems.
method: Analytical and numerical analysis of a queueing model where the arrival process is a search with resetting in an interval, deriving conditions for instability.
result: Stochastic resetting can induce queue instability even when the underlying search process would otherwise be stable, with critical resetting rates identified.
conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of resetting dynamics in queueing theory, with potential applications to biological and engineered systems, though further work is needed for realistic scenarios.

conclusion: The method offers a way to infer causal structure in stochastic systems, with potential applications in physics and neuroscience, but is not directly related to the user's research interests.

conclusion: The findings provide insights into Bose-Einstein condensation in confined geometries, relevant for ultracold atomic gases in nanostructures.

conclusion: The model provides insights into how social pressure and individual conviction shape public discourse, with potential applications to understanding political polls, social media dynamics, and collective behavior.

method: The authors propose a bidirectional causal neural stochastic differential equation (SDE) model that learns forward and backward dynamics from snapshot data, incorporating cell type information and handling nonsteady-state rotational effects.
result: The method reconstructs continuous cell trajectories and gene regulatory interactions from snapshots, outperforming existing approaches on synthetic and real datasets.
conclusion: This work provides a powerful tool for inferring cellular dynamics from destructive measurements, with potential applications in developmental biology and disease modeling.

conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for understanding active matter in anisotropic environments, with implications for biological and synthetic active systems.

tldr: The paper introduces 'super-resonance' as a phenomenon that overcomes the bandwidth limit of resonant modes, with an application to flow control.
motivation: To break the inherent bandwidth limitation of conventional resonance, enabling broadband out-of-phase response for applications like flow stabilization.
method: Theoretical analysis and possibly numerical simulations of a resonant system designed to achieve super-resonance.
result: Super-resonance maintains a broadband out-of-phase response beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance.

tldr: This paper reports nonlinear magnetic susceptibility measurements in a kagome spin ice compound, revealing hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking via a three-dimensional XY universality class transition.
motivation: To investigate the nature of the ground state and phase transition in the kagome spin ice HoAgGe, particularly regarding time-reversal symmetry breaking.

result: The ground state exhibits hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking, and the transition belongs to the three-dimensional XY universality class.
conclusion: The findings provide insight into frustrated magnetism and may inform studies of topological phases, but are not directly relevant to the user's research interests.

tldr: This paper reports the discovery of robust orbital-selective flat bands in layered transition-metal oxyhalides that persist at room temperature, as observed by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.
motivation: To find and characterize materials with intrinsic flat bands that are stable at room temperature, providing a platform for studying strongly correlated electron physics without the need for extreme conditions.
method: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) was used to measure the electronic band structure of layered transition-metal oxyhalides, revealing flat bands. Theoretical calculations likely supported the interpretation.
result: Intrinsic flat bands were observed that remain stable at room temperature, with orbital-selective character, offering a tunable system for exploring correlated states.
conclusion: These materials provide a new platform for investigating strongly correlated electron phenomena at accessible temperatures, with potential for future studies of exotic phases like superconductivity or magnetism.

method: Experimental characterization of elastic and structural properties of silica thin films using techniques such as Brillouin light scattering and X-ray diffraction.
result: Silica films exhibit hidden anisotropy that is not removed by standard heat treatment, affecting their elastic behavior.
conclusion: The findings inform coating design and deposition strategies to reduce thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors.

abstract:
Author(s): Shang Gao, Hao Shang, Hao Hu, Yu-Qiang Ma, and Qun-Li Lei

Where ordinary fluids show wild fluctuations and critical opalescence, hyperuniform fluids of spinning particles stay unusually calm yet highly susceptible at the liquid–vapor critical point.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021032] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the critical behavior of hyperuniform fluids at the liquid-gas phase transition, focusing on suppressed density fluctuations.
motivation: To understand how hyperuniformity, a state with suppressed long-wavelength density fluctuations, affects critical phenomena in fluids.
method: Theoretical analysis and possibly simulations of a model of spinning particles that exhibit hyperuniformity near the liquid-vapor critical point.
result: Hyperuniform fluids show anomalously low density fluctuations at the critical point while maintaining high susceptibility, leading to unique critical exponents.
conclusion: The findings reveal a new class of critical behavior and may have implications for designing materials with tailored fluctuation properties.

[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021028] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: Experiments on two-dimensional photonic crystals reveal unexpected residual scattering in stealthy hyperuniform materials due to radiative loss.
motivation: To test the predicted transparency of disordered stealthy hyperuniform materials in a specific wavelength range.
method: Large-scale silicon photonic crystals were fabricated and optical transmission/scattering measurements were performed.
result: Contrary to expectations, significant residual scattering was observed, attributed to radiative loss mechanisms.
conclusion: The findings challenge the ideal transparency assumption and highlight the role of radiative losses in hyperuniform photonic systems.

motivation: To directly observe and characterize ion diffusion in superionic conductors at ultrafast timescales, linking microscopic dynamics to macroscopic properties for better material design.

result: Direct spatial and temporal mapping of ion diffusion pathways and rates in AgCrSe2.
conclusion: Provides a new experimental approach to study ion dynamics, with implications for designing high-performance superionic conductors.

result: The authors identify a dipolar nematic ordering that underpins the relaxor behavior, providing new insights into the microscopic structure.

abstract:

By combining experiments with robotic metamaterials and theory, this work shows that increasing microscopic activity can counterintuitively cause a solid’s macroscale active response to vanish when active units are too sparse for the active forces to percolate through the structure.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021012] Published Mon Apr 13, 2026.
tldr: Increasing microscopic activity in unpercolated active solids can counterintuitively cause the macroscopic active response to vanish.
motivation: To understand how the density of active units affects the collective mechanical response in active solids, particularly when active forces are too sparse to percolate.
method: Combined experiments with robotic metamaterials and theoretical modeling to study the effect of activity on macroscopic response.
result: Found that beyond a certain threshold, increasing activity reduces the overall active response due to lack of percolation of active forces.
conclusion: The work reveals a 'more is less' phenomenon in active solids, with implications for designing materials with tunable mechanical properties.

result: Subsurface compliant regions in nanodiamond enable size-dependent elastic response, allowing diamond to deform elastically under strain.
conclusion: The findings provide a method to engineer mechanical properties of brittle materials like diamond, with potential applications in nanomechanics and materials science.

motivation: To understand how mechanical forces and flows drive chromatin organization within the nucleus, which is crucial for gene regulation and cellular function.

result: The model shows that active stresses and flows can lead to spontaneous segregation of euchromatin and heterochromatin, reproducing nucleus-wide patterns observed in experiments.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the role of surface defects and plasma formation.
motivation: To understand and mitigate vacuum breakdown that limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-voltage vacuum devices.
method: Review of experimental observations and computer simulations to build a mechanistic picture of breakdown initiation.
result: Breakdown is triggered by complex interactions between surface defects, electric stress, heating, and emitted particles.
conclusion: Improved understanding can lead to more reliable and efficient high-power technologies and advanced accelerators.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the history and scientific legacy of the Arecibo 305-m radio telescope, highlighting its contributions to pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave detection.
motivation: To provide a historical perspective on Arecibo's impact on radio astronomy and its enduring legacy after its collapse.
method: Historical review and synthesis of major scientific results obtained with the Arecibo telescope over its operational lifetime.
result: Arecibo made pioneering contributions across diverse fields including pulsar timing, neutral hydrogen mapping, VLBI imaging, SETI, and the first detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.
conclusion: The telescope's upgrades and unique capabilities enabled transformative science; its legacy continues through data archives and future radio observatories.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the prospects for multimessenger astronomy using continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and future detectors.
motivation: To discuss detection prospects for continuous gravitational waves and their connection to electromagnetic observations, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics.
method: Review and survey of theoretical and observational prospects for continuous gravitational wave detection with next-generation detectors.
result: The paper outlines the potential for multimessenger observations to inform understanding of dense matter and neutron star physics.
conclusion: Continuous gravitational waves offer a new window into neutron star interiors, but direct relevance to the user's research interests in quantum information thermodynamics, foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems is minimal.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses how gravitational-wave and X-ray observations of neutron stars constrain the dense matter equation of state.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities, which is key for nuclear physics and astrophysics.
method: Review of observational data from binary neutron star mergers (gravitational waves) and X-ray pulse profile measurements, compared to nuclear theory predictions.
result: Observations provide constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, which test nuclear equation of state models.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine the equation of state and may reveal exotic matter phases.

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030502] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: Geoffrey Hinton's Nobel lecture reviews the history and principles of Boltzmann machines, a class of stochastic neural networks.
motivation: The lecture was given upon receiving the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics, summarizing Hinton's contributions to machine learning.
method: The paper is a transcript of the Nobel lecture, describing the conceptual development and training algorithms for Boltzmann machines.
result: The lecture explains how Boltzmann machines learn internal representations and their connection to statistical physics.
conclusion: Boltzmann machines have influenced deep learning but are not directly related to the user's research interests in quantum information and thermodynamics.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: This review covers atomic-scale microscopy techniques for measuring disorder in semiconductors, with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand how atomic-scale disorder affects semiconductor properties, which is important for materials science but not for the user's research interests.
method: Review of three real-space techniques: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, applied to compound semiconductors.
result: The techniques can reveal atomic-scale disorder, and combining them provides a more complete picture of defects.
conclusion: The paper is a materials science review with no implications for quantum computing, thermodynamics, or quantum communication.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: This review summarizes the quantum-mechanical phenomena governing low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and new experimental approaches to study them.
motivation: To understand stellar burning and element formation, which require knowledge of nuclear reactions at very low energies that are difficult to measure directly.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes theoretical developments in low-energy nuclear reaction theory, including tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discusses new experimental ideas.
result: The review presents the state of the art in theory and describes novel methods for measuring these reactions on Earth.
conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive overview that may guide future research in nuclear astrophysics, but it is not directly related to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: This review explores self-alignment in polar active matter, where particles align their orientation with their velocity, leading to novel collective behaviors.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment, as opposed to neighbor imitation, shapes motion in active systems and to unify existing models.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes existing models and experiments on self-alignment in active matter, providing a conceptual and mathematical framework.
result: Self-alignment enables phenomena such as orbiting in traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, fundamentally altering collective dynamics.
conclusion: The framework offers insights for biology, smart materials, and robotics, and suggests new directions for studying active systems.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique using laser-induced ultrasound, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To provide an overview of optoacoustic imaging methods and their applications in biological and clinical research.
method: Review of basic physics, impact on research, and latest developments in multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: Optoacoustic imaging offers noninvasive, high-resolution imaging at depths of millimeters to centimeters using optical contrast.
conclusion: The method is valuable for biological and clinical imaging, but the paper does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Wrinkles, Creases, And Cusps In Growing Soft Matter
authors: Martine Ben Amar
abstract:
Author(s): Martine Ben Amar

The buckling of a material surface subject to compression or growth is a ubiquitous phenomenon, arising in materials science contexts such as the swelling of gels as well as in biological contexts such as morphogenesis and embryogenesis. A complete understanding of the creases and sharp cusps that commonly accompany buckling requires nonlinear elasticity theory. This review presents a modern treatment of the Biot instability, integrating many standard techniques of nonlinear physics and solid mechanics, such as bifurcation theory, conformal mapping, and
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015004] Published Mon Feb 24, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nonlinear elasticity theory for buckling, creases, and cusps in growing soft matter, with applications in gels and biological morphogenesis.
motivation: To provide a modern treatment of the Biot instability and understand creases and cusps that accompany buckling in soft materials.
method: Integrates bifurcation theory, conformal mapping, and nonlinear physics techniques to analyze instabilities.
result: Presents a comprehensive review of nonlinear elasticity approaches to buckling and pattern formation in growing soft matter.
conclusion: The work consolidates standard techniques for studying instabilities, with implications for materials science and developmental biology.

title: Using Gravitational Waves To See The First Second Of The Universe
authors: Rishav Roshan And Graham White
abstract:
Author(s): Rishav Roshan and Graham White

Gravitational waves open a unique window on the earliest times in cosmology because the dense primordial plasma, impenetrable to light or neutrinos, is transparent to gravitational waves up to the instant of the birth of the Universe. This review discusses the possible signals from the phase transitions, topological defects, and other cosmological sources, as well as a range of strategies for detection of the stochastic gravitational waves produced by the earliest events in the history of the Universe.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015001] Published Wed Jan 08, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses how gravitational waves from the early universe can probe the first second after the Big Bang, focusing on phase transitions and topological defects.
motivation: To explore gravitational waves as a tool to study the earliest moments of the universe, which are inaccessible via electromagnetic radiation.
method: Review of theoretical models and detection strategies for stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds from cosmological sources.
result: Identifies phase transitions and topological defects as key sources of gravitational waves in the early universe.
conclusion: Gravitational wave astronomy can provide unique insights into the first second of cosmic history, with future detectors potentially observing these signals.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: This review describes the ecosystem of software tools for constructing and using Wannier functions in materials simulations.
motivation: Wannier functions provide a localized real-space representation of electronic structure, enabling efficient calculations and deeper insights. The review aims to document the growing interoperable software ecosystem that supports these methods.
method: The paper is a review that surveys various software packages and methodologies for Wannier function generation and application, including their interoperability and use in computing properties like topological invariants.
result: The review catalogs the current state of the Wannier-function software ecosystem, highlighting key tools and their capabilities.
conclusion: The ecosystem has become a major instrument for electronic-structure research, enabling advanced materials simulations and design.

title: Kinetic Solitary Electrostatic Structures In Collisionless Plasma: Phase-space Holes
authors: I. H. Hutchinson
abstract:
Author(s): I. H. Hutchinson

Plasma is usually taught to be a quasineutral gas of charged and neutral particles that exhibits collective behavior. However, satellites regularly observe solitary potential structures in space plasmas that are isolated positive or negative potential humps, called electron or ion holes. In the 1970s, laboratory observations were made of electron holes. This review presents an overview of the observation of these electrostatic structures and presents their origin and their stability, using analytic theory and simulations. The role of kinetically unstable velocity distributions is identified as a key driver.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045007] Published Tue Dec 10, 2024.
tldr: This paper reviews kinetic solitary electrostatic structures (electron and ion holes) in collisionless plasma, focusing on their observation, origin, and stability.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of phase-space holes in plasma, which are commonly observed in space plasmas but not fully understood.
method: The review synthesizes analytic theory, simulations, and observational data from satellites and laboratory experiments.
result: Identifies kinetically unstable velocity distributions as key drivers for the formation of electron and ion holes.
conclusion: The paper consolidates current understanding and highlights open questions about the stability and dynamics of these structures.

title: Evolutionary Vaccination Dynamics Under Higher-order Reinforcement Pressure
authors: Yikang Lu, Ying Wang, Alfonso de Miguel-Arribas, Lei Shi And Yamir Moreno
abstract: Vaccination games in higher-order settings remain underexplored, despite their importance in shaping opinions and collective decisions. Here, we introduce a parsimonious behavioral-epidemiological model to evaluate how peer reinforcement influences vaccination uptake. The framework consists of a two-layer multiplex: an epidemic layer governed by the susceptible-infected-recovered process on a square lattice, and a behavioral layer represented by a hypergraph of triadic interactions. Individuals update their vaccination strategy via imitation, modulated by a reinforcement modulation parameter when local agreement with a like-minded peer is present. We find that higher-order structure alone induces clusters of vaccinated individuals that act as protective barriers. Small but nonzero values of ( ) maximize vaccination coverage and suppress outbreaks, while both the limiting case and larger values ( ) reduce uptake. This non-monotonic effect suggests that excessively strong local inhibition suppresses adaptability, whereas weaker inhibition facilitates the re-emergence of non-vaccinators. Our work bridges complex contagion theory with evolutionary game dynamics, offering insights into how contact structure and peer reinforcement jointly shape vaccination behavior.
tldr: This paper studies vaccination behavior on a multiplex network with higher-order social interactions, finding that moderate peer reinforcement maximizes vaccine uptake.
motivation: To understand how higher-order social interactions (triadic) influence vaccination decisions, which is underexplored in vaccination games.
method: A two-layer multiplex model combining an SIR epidemic on a square lattice with a hypergraph for behavioral imitation, modulated by a reinforcement parameter.
result: Higher-order structure alone creates protective clusters; small reinforcement maximizes coverage and suppresses outbreaks, while zero or large reinforcement reduces uptake.
conclusion: The work bridges complex contagion and evolutionary game dynamics, suggesting that moderate local inhibition is optimal for vaccination behavior.

title: Electric-field-driven Nanoconfinement And The 5–120 Nm Stability Regime Of Piezoelectric Β-glycine
authors: Kexin Zhang And Zhengbao Yang
abstract: Piezoelectric β-glycine is a promising molecular crystal, yet its controlled preparation remains challenging. Current nanoconfinement strategies, which rely primarily on rigid templates or simulations, cannot reliably capture the intrinsic confinement regime that leads to β-phase formation. Here, we propose electric-field-driven nanoconfinement as a one-step, continuous, and interface-free approach to investigate glycine crystallization and to define the confinement regime that yields the β-phase. We produced glycine nanoparticles via electrohydrodynamic spraying under a direct current field, automatically varying the spraying height to modulate nanoconfinement during nucleation and growth. Structural, morphological, and piezoelectric characterizations reveal that pure β-glycine forms within a crystal radius range of 5–120 nm. By integrating these findings with thermodynamic and kinetic analysis, we elucidate the mechanism of β-phase formation and construct a crystallization phase map that delineates the confinement conditions necessary for its stabilization. This work identifies the critical nanoconfinement parameters for accessing piezoelectric β-glycine and provides fundamental insights into polymorph control in molecular crystalline materials.
tldr: This paper investigates electric-field-driven nanoconfinement to stabilize piezoelectric β-glycine nanocrystals within a 5–120 nm size range.
motivation: Controlled preparation of piezoelectric β-glycine is challenging; existing nanoconfinement methods cannot reliably capture the intrinsic confinement regime for β-phase formation.
method: Electrohydrodynamic spraying under a DC field was used to produce glycine nanoparticles, with spraying height varied to modulate nanoconfinement during nucleation and growth.
result: Pure β-glycine forms within a crystal radius range of 5–120 nm; a crystallization phase map delineating confinement conditions for β-phase stabilization was constructed.
conclusion: This work identifies critical nanoconfinement parameters for accessing piezoelectric β-glycine and provides insights into polymorph control in molecular crystals.

title: Visualizing Lattice-mismatch-dependent Strain Relaxation In Epitaxially Grown MoS2/WS2 And MoS2/WSe2 Hetero-bilayers
authors: Jinwoo Kim, Ingyu Yoo, Jaewoong Joo, Hyoungseok Lee, Jundong Yeo, Jian-Min Zuo, Miyoung Kim And Gwan-Hyoung Lee
abstract: Strain relaxation at lattice-mismatched interfaces is critical for epitaxial growth and high-quality single-crystal films. While van der Waals (vdW) epitaxy is considered as a promising platform due to its high tolerance to lattice mismatch, its actual response to lattice mismatch remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate the effect of lattice mismatch on vdW interfaces by epitaxially growing MoS2 on WS2 or WSe2 substrate. annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy reveals that MoS2/WS2 with a negligible lattice mismatch of ∼0.22% forms a fully commensurate structure, whereas MoS2/WSe2 with a large lattice mismatch of ∼3.96% exhibits non-uniform moiré patterns, characteristic of an incommensurate interface. Detailed analysis shows that the MoS2/WS2 hetero-bilayers exhibit perfectly aligned structure through compression of MoS2, whereas the MoS2/WSe2 hetero-bilayers show elongation and rotation of moiré orientation driven by tensile strain. Notably, even small twist angles induce significant changes in moiré orientation, resulting in bent fringes that are indicative of local rotational distortions. Large lattice mismatch drives localized lattice distortion, where rotation of the MoS2 lattice emerges as an energetically favorable mechanism for strain release, in contrast to commensurate alignment in small-mismatch systems. Our results establish moiré pattern analysis as a powerful framework for directly visualizing spatially varying strain and its relaxation pathways in vdW hetero-bilayers. Our work reveals previously inaccessible interfacial deformation modes in vdW hetero-bilayers and establishes moiré analysis as a powerful platform for strain engineering in 2D electronic and optoelectronic materials.
tldr: This paper studies strain relaxation in MoS2/WS2 and MoS2/WSe2 hetero-bilayers using microscopy, focusing on lattice mismatch effects in van der Waals epitaxy.
motivation: To understand how lattice mismatch influences strain relaxation in van der Waals heterostructures, which is critical for epitaxial growth and device quality.
method: Epitaxial growth of MoS2 on WS2 or WSe2 substrates, followed by annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (ADF-STEM) to image moiré patterns and analyze lattice distortions.
result: Small mismatch (0.22%) yields fully commensurate structure via compression; large mismatch (3.96%) leads to incommensurate moiré patterns with elongation, rotation, and bent fringes, indicating local rotational distortions as a strain release mechanism.
conclusion: Moiré pattern analysis is a powerful tool for visualizing strain relaxation in 2D heterostructures, enabling strain engineering for electronic and optoelectronic applications.

authors: Guillem Domènech, Shi Pi (皮石), And Ao Wang

The ambiguity in associating gravitational waves with transverse-traceless components of the metric at second order in perturbation theory is resolved by computing the detector response to second order for the first time.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 221402] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: The paper resolves an ambiguity in associating gravitational waves with transverse-traceless metric components at second order by computing the detector response to second order.
motivation: To clarify the interpretation of gravitational wave signals at second order in perturbation theory, where the standard transverse-traceless decomposition is ambiguous.
method: The authors compute the detector response to second order in perturbation theory, providing a direct observable that resolves the ambiguity.
result: They show that the detector response at second order is well-defined and can be used to unambiguously identify gravitational wave strain.
conclusion: This work provides a rigorous foundation for interpreting second-order gravitational wave signals, which is important for future observations.

Conventional one-dimensional (1D) Brownian motion on surfaces relies on physical tracks such as prefabricated channels or grooves. Here, we demonstrate through molecular dynamics simulations that a monolayer polymeric [MATH] nanoflake can undergo persistent 1D Brownian motion on unpatte…

motivation: To explore whether one-dimensional Brownian motion can occur on surfaces without predefined tracks, challenging the conventional need for physical confinement.
method: Molecular dynamics simulations of a monolayer polymeric nanoflake on a two-dimensional crystal surface.
result: The nanoflake exhibits persistent one-dimensional Brownian motion on the unpatterned surface, suggesting that intrinsic surface properties can guide motion.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium decays and new hadron searches.
motivation: To understand strong interaction mechanisms like quark confinement and gluon binding by studying charmonium decays and searching for new hadrons.
method: Review of experimental results from BaBar, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII on hadron production in e+e- collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs.
result: BESIII has become the leading facility for high-precision measurements in this area, with recent advances highlighted.
conclusion: Continued experimental progress will provide deeper insights into QCD and hadron spectroscopy.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the scientific legacy of the Arecibo planetary radar system, focusing on observations of Solar System bodies and near-Earth asteroids.
motivation: To provide an overview of the contributions of the Arecibo radar system to planetary science, particularly after its upgrade in the late 1990s until its collapse in 2020.
method: The paper is a review summarizing key observations and techniques of planetary radar, including delay-Doppler imaging and radar spectroscopy.
result: Arecibo radar provided unique insights into the surfaces and subsurfaces of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, Saturn's moons, and numerous near-Earth asteroids and comets.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system was a unique and powerful tool for planetary science, and its loss leaves a gap that future missions and instruments may partially fill.

abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews advances in geospace science achieved using the Arecibo Observatory's radar, lidar, and optical instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: To summarize key scientific contributions from the Arecibo Observatory's unique capabilities in studying the upper atmosphere and ionosphere.
method: Review of incoherent scatter radar technique and results from Arecibo's suite of instruments, including lidars and optical sensors, combined with satellite data.
result: Highlights advances in plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.
conclusion: The paper underscores the legacy of Arecibo in geospace science but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, or related topics.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This colloquium reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds, focusing on droplet growth via condensation and collision-coalescence.
motivation: The rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is poorly understood theoretically; controlled experiments are needed to resolve this bottleneck.
method: The paper reviews experimental, theoretical, and computational studies using convection-cloud chambers that reproduce turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation.
result: Convection-cloud chambers can capture key cloud processes and bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales, providing insights into the precipitation bottleneck.
conclusion: The approach offers a promising path to understanding warm-rain formation, but further integration of experiments, theory, and models is required.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae and their detection in multimessenger astronomy.
motivation: To summarize progress in modeling core collapse supernovae and predicting gravitational wave signals for upcoming observations.
method: Review of core collapse supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, along with detection methods for ground-based interferometers.
result: Latest progress in supernova modeling and associated gravitational wave signatures are presented.
conclusion: Detection of gravitational waves from a Galactic supernova would provide unique insights into the supernova engine and neutron star physics.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a potential challenge to the cosmological principle and ΛCDM model, based on discrepancies between matter distribution dipoles and the CMB dipole.
motivation: To test the cosmological principle by comparing the dipole in large-scale structure with the CMB dipole, which is assumed to arise from our peculiar motion in ΛCDM.
method: Analysis of large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars to measure the dipole in matter distribution and compare it with the CMB dipole, including assessment of biases and systematics.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the matter dipole and the CMB dipole, suggesting a possible violation of the cosmological principle.
conclusion: The anomaly may challenge the standard ΛCDM model, warranting further investigation into systematic effects or alternative cosmological models.

abstract:

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.

method: The paper is a review that surveys experimental constraints from LHC Run 2 and theoretical developments, and projects discovery potential for the HL-LHC across multiple search channels and supersymmetric scenarios.
result: The review identifies remaining viable supersymmetric models and provides projections for HL-LHC sensitivity, but does not present new experimental data or theoretical breakthroughs.
conclusion: The HL-LHC will significantly extend the reach for supersymmetry, but the paper does not directly address the user's research interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, quantum communication, or hybrid quantum systems.

abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.
